title: Education at Shinnecock
summary: Shinnecock education connects community teaching, the reservation school, Native educators, state responsibility, and students' continuing pursuit of learning.
content:
Education at Shinnecock has taken place through families, community knowledge, churches, teachers, and formal schools. Lois Marie Hunter's 1950 account treats the reservation school as a Shinnecock institution even while describing the unequal state system that supplied its building and teachers.

The reservation school

Hunter wrote that Shinnecock provided land for a state-supported school and that New York supplied the building and teachers through June 30, 1950. Her account says the school burned in 1875; the project's reviewed chronology separates the 1874 fire from the replacement school opened in 1875. During that transition, Rebecca Bunn—remembered as Aunt Becky—taught Shinnecock children. The history is kept at reservation level rather than assigning a precise school map point from this source alone.1

A 1950 snapshot

By 1950, Hunter described a two-teacher elementary school while high-school students traveled to Southampton by bus. She also remembered Native ministers and other teachers contributing to education, including Thomas H. Williams, whose later farming work connected teaching, land, and family economy. Hunter's account shows education as both an institution and a continuing community responsibility.
